gd.officer.title: How to use TerraOrb for Officers
gd.officer.intro: This guide is for agricultural officers and instructors who watch many tanks at once. Start by signing in with the phone number your office registered; the dashboard then shows every tank on one screen.
gd.officer.signin.name: Officer sign-in
gd.officer.signin.what: The dashboard opens only for registered officers. You sign in with your phone number and a short one-time code. No password.
gd.officer.signin.step1: Open the Dashboard page from the menu.
gd.officer.signin.step2: Type the phone number your office registered and tap "Send me a code".
gd.officer.signin.step3: Type the code and tap "Sign in". The dashboard opens.
gd.officer.signin.step4: When you finish, tap "Sign out" at the top.
gd.officer.signin.tip: If it says the number is not registered as an officer, ask your office to add it. Sign-in protects the dashboard screen only; the tank data files themselves are public.
gd.officer.dashboard.name: All tanks at a glance
gd.officer.dashboard.what: One row for every tank: the signal, tank water against usual, rain this season, when the rains started, forecast rain and how green the land is.
gd.officer.dashboard.step1: Sign in and open the Dashboard.
gd.officer.dashboard.step2: Read the Signal column: Good, Be careful, Too little water or Not checked yet.
gd.officer.dashboard.step3: Compare "Water vs usual", "Rain this season vs usual" and "Rains started" to see which tanks are behind.
gd.officer.dashboard.step4: Tap a tank name to open its full advice page.
gd.officer.dashboard.tip: A dash means there is no number yet; nothing is guessed. Rain is NASA POWER, tank water is NASA OPERA/HLS satellites (measured for few tanks so far), greenness is NASA MODIS. The 7-day forecast and the live "next 6 hours" rain are Open-Meteo, not NASA data.
gd.officer.filters.name: Filter, search and sort
gd.officer.filters.what: Find the tanks that need a visit first, in seconds, without scrolling through the whole list.
gd.officer.filters.step1: Tap a signal box at the top to show only those tanks. Tap "All tanks" to clear it.
gd.officer.filters.step2: Type a name in "Find a tank".
gd.officer.filters.step3: Choose "Sort by": Signal (worst first), Name, Water (lowest first) or Forecast rain (most first).
gd.officer.filters.step4: Tick "Hide demo tanks" to remove the demonstration tanks.
gd.officer.filters.tip: The "Heavy rain soon" box (30 mm in 6 hours) appears only when the live rain has loaded. It is a live weather-model forecast from Open-Meteo, not NASA data, and forecasts are never certain. The 30 mm level is a draft.
gd.officer.report.name: CSV and printed report
gd.officer.report.what: Take the table with you: a CSV file for your spreadsheet, or a clean printed report of the tanks on screen.
gd.officer.report.step1: Use the filters to show the tanks you want in the report.
gd.officer.report.step2: Tap "Download CSV" to save those rows for Excel or another spreadsheet.
gd.officer.report.step3: Tap "Print report" and print it or save it as a PDF.
gd.officer.report.step4: Check the date line at the top of the report: it shows when it was printed and when the data was updated.
gd.officer.report.tip: The CSV and the report contain only the rows currently shown, and the source note is printed under the table. Demo tanks are marked, so hide them before you share.
gd.officer.national.name: Country-level NASA data
gd.officer.national.what: Under the tank table: fires seen from space (NASA FIRMS), water stored in the ground (NASA GRACE-FO) and a NASA map of floods and cloud.
gd.officer.national.step1: Scroll below the tank table to "Country-level NASA data".
gd.officer.national.step2: Read "Fires seen from space": the hot spots NASA satellites saw in Sri Lanka, with date, place and fire power.
gd.officer.national.step3: Read "Stored water in the ground": the latest month against the usual for that month since 2018.
gd.officer.national.step4: On the map, tap the layers button (top right) to show NASA flood water, cloud cover or satellite pictures. Red dots are fire detections.
gd.officer.national.tip: A hot spot may be a wildfire, burning stubble or a kiln, and no fire detected does not prove none burned. The groundwater figure is one coarse measurement (about 300 km) for the whole country, not for wells or farms. If a data file is missing, the card says so.
